newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Sept 12.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Sept 12.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- PRU'S DAVIS RULES OUT 'SILLY PRICE' FOR SOCIETY

As the Prudential, Britain's biggest insurance company, turned in interim operating profits ahead of expectations it dampened speculation that the group was about to acquire a building society. The group has made no secret of its desire to acquire a life company or building society. However, Peter Davis, chief executive, warned the company would not pay a "silly price" but would build up a branch network from its telephone banking operation.
-- LABOUR PLANS VOTES ON FAT CAT SALARIES

The Labour Party has declared that it would introduce legislation giving shareholders the right to vote on pay packages in an attempt to end the confusion over its efforts to curb "fat cat" salaries. There have been suggestions of a climbdown after shadow chancellor Gordon Brown and shadow chief secretary Alistair Darling indicated Labour would place the emphasis on changing corporate behaviour through voluntary reforms rather that legislation.
-- ASDA ASDD.L TO TAKE ON 3,000 STAFF

Asda, the supermarket group, has announced plans to recruit about 3,000 staff as it prepares to open six stores in the first half of next year and refurbish a further 30. The opening plan is described by the group as being "a modest acceleration" from its programme this year. Patrick Gillam, chairman, said he would sustain the group's attack on resale price maintenance on over- the-counter medicines by announcing the launch of an own-brand folic acid.
THE TIMES
-- HANSON BRICK TO SET UP WORKS COUNCIL

One of the biggest Conservative Party supporters, Hanson, is preparing to set up a European works council. The deal comes a day after Lord Hanson condemned the European Union's social chapter from which the Government opted-out to avoid requirements including European-style employee consultation. The deal is in Hanson's brick division and is hailed by union leaders as a big step towards the acceptance of works councils, which have been adopted by more than 100 UK companies.
-- REUTERS PLANS 613 MILLION STG PAYOUT TO INVESTORS

The financial information and trading group, Reuters, is set to use its cash reserves of 613 million stg to pay shareholders through the issue of special dividend shares, over three years. The scheme raises the total cash returned to shareholders to almost one billion stg. Investors welcomed the news as shares rose. Shareholders will receive 19 new ordinary shares and one special dividend share for every 20 shares held on October eighth.
-- GOVERNMENT WARNING ON "JOB-DESTROYING POLICIES'

The 15,600 fall in unemployment has been seized on by the British Government as a warning against the adoption of policies that would destroy jobs. Employment and Education Minister, Cheryl Gillan, has said that the further fall in unemployment in August combined with stable earnings growth and low inflation make the UK the most successful major economy in Europe. She warned against the effects of the introduction of a statutory national minimum wage.
THE GUARDIAN
-- CUT-PRICE FLOTATION MEANS BIG BONUS FOR THISTLE CHIEF

Chief executive of Thistle Hotels, Robert Peel, is in line for a cash bonus of 500,000 stg when the company comes to market, while senior operations director Norbert Peterson will receive 250,000 stg. The company also confirmed the depressed state of the new issues market and said it would be valued at just over one billion stg at its flotation next month, below initial forecasts of 1.5 billion stg.
-- DE BENEDETTI HOLDINGS FACE BOURSE INQUIRY

COB, the Bourse watchdog has opened an inquiry following press accounts of a planned deal involving a French holding company owned by Carlo De Benedetti, former chairman of Olivetti, and another French group. The watchdog has started its inquiry on reports that the French group CGIP would take over Cerus, the De Benedetti investment vehicle, and Valeo, a car-parts maker that Cerus controls. These coincided with evidence in Italy that De Benedetti's main holding company, CIR, had pledged about two-thirds of its 14.44 per cent of shares in Olivetti to Chase Manhattan Bank as collateral for a loan of 300 billion lire.
-- MAGNATE DENIES PLOTTING 1.2 BILLION DOLLAR FRAUD THAT LED TO BCCI COLLAPSE

The Old Bailey has heard that Abbas Gokal, head of an international shipping and trading empire plotted a 1.2 billion dollar fraud that led to the collapse of BCCI bank and financial disaster for its depositors. According to prosecuting QC, Anthony Hacking, Mr Gokal operated the swindle to fund his lavish life-style and provide personal gain for himself and his family. The hearing is expected to last six months.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- DEUTSCHE FOOTS BILL FOR MORGAN BONUS BONANZA

The German bank behind the three Morgan Asset Management funds, Deutsche Bank, is expected to pay millions of pounds stg of bonuses to fund managers in spite of enormous losses. The bonuses will help Morgan retail its fund management team and improve morale, after funds were suspended due to the activities of fund manager Peter Young. Deutsche Bank has committed itself to further protection of funds by promising to buy units in the two trusts affected, European Growth Trust and Europa, and shares in European Capital Growth Fund.
-- OFGAS LIKELY TO PHASE IN SUPPLIERS

The gas industry watchdog, Ofgas, has given a clear signal that it would phase in the move towards full competition for domestic customers, instead of throwing the market open in one move in the spring of 1998. This raises the possibility of delays for some of the more than 16 million affected households, which might not be able to shop around for alternative gas supplies to British Gas until the end of 1998 at least.
-- GRID INVESTORS PROTEST AT NEW PRICE REGIME

Professor Littlechild, the electricity regulator, has received protests about proposed new price controls from investors holding up to a third ot the shares in the National Grid. Leading fund managers have urged the Grid to take the dispute to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission if Offer, the watchdog, refuses to water down the four-year price regime when the final formula is unveiled this month.
